title: The Seven Chords of a Key
description: Build a chord on every note of C major and meet the family most songs are written with.

steps.title: One chord per note
steps.description:
Take the C major scale, start on any note, and stack every other white key on top: play one, skip one, play one. You get seven chords:

• I = C (major)
• ii = Dm (minor)
• iii = Em (minor)
• IV = F (major)
• V = G (major)
• vi = Am (minor)
• vii° = Bdim (diminished)

Capital numerals are major, small ones are minor. The pattern is the same in every major key, so once you know it here, you know it everywhere.

steps.title: I, C major
steps.description: This is home. Most songs in C start here and end here, and it's the chord that sounds most at rest.

steps.title: ii, D minor
steps.description: Slide the whole shape up one white key. The ii chord loves to lead into V. Jazz players lean on that ii-V-I move all the time.
steps.hint: D, F, A. Same skip-a-key shape, one step up.

steps.title: iii, E minor
steps.description: Up one more. E minor shares two notes with C major, so it can stand in for the I chord with a slightly wistful colour.

steps.title: IV, F major
steps.description: The IV chord feels like stepping out the front door. It's one of the three chords you'll find in countless folk, rock and blues songs.

steps.title: V, G major
steps.description: The V chord pulls hardest back toward I. Play G, then play C right after it and you'll feel the release.

steps.title: vi, A minor
steps.description: A minor is C major's relative minor. Put it in the order I-V-vi-IV (C, G, Am, F) and you've got the progression behind a huge number of pop songs.

steps.title: vii°, B diminished
steps.description: The odd one out. B diminished is tense and doesn't get used much on its own, but its B wants to step up to C, so it leans hard toward home.
steps.hint: B, D, F. Still all white keys.

steps.title: The minor ones
steps.description: In any major key, which three chords are minor?
